blocks.text: K. considered whether he ought not to leave with all haste now; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect of his being able to do so during the sermon, he would then have to remain as long as it lasted, he was losing so much time at the office, he had long since ceased to be obliged to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was eleven. But could a sermon really be preached? Could K. alone constitute the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who merely wished to see the church? At bottom he was nothing else. It was absurd to think that a sermon was to be preached, now at eleven o’clock, on a weekday in the most atrocious weather. The priest—there was no doubt that he was a priest, a young man with a smooth, dark face—was plainly going up merely to extinguish the lamp, which had been lit by mistake.

But this was not so, the priest instead examined the light and turned it up a little further, then slowly turned towards the parapet, taking hold of its angular rim in front with both hands. Thus he stood for a while and looked about him without moving his head. K. had retreated a considerable distance and was leaning with his elbows on the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw the verger somewhere, without being able to determine the spot exactly, crouching down with his back bent, peacefully, as though his task were done. What silence now reigned in the cathedral! But K. had to disturb it, he had no intention of remaining here; if it was the priest’s duty to preach at a particular hour regardless of circumstances, then let him do so, he would succeed even without K.’s assistance, just as K.’s presence would certainly not heighten the effect. So K. slowly set off, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, then reached the broad central aisle and walked there too quite undisturbed, except that the stone floor rang beneath the lightest footfall and the vaulting echoed it faintly but ceaselessly in a manifold, measured progression. K. felt a little forsaken as he walked there alone between the empty pews, perhaps observed by the priest, and the size of the cathedral seemed to him to lie just at the limit of what human beings could still endure. When he reached his former place, he fairly snatched up the album he had left lying there without pausing further and took it with him. He had almost left the region of the pews and was approaching the open space between them and the exit when he heard the priest’s voice for the first time. A powerful, practised voice. How it penetrated the cathedral, which stood ready to receive it! But it was not the congregation that the priest addressed, it was quite unmistakable and there was no evading it, he called: “Josef K.!”

K. stopped short and looked at the floor before him. For the present he was still free, he could still walk on and make his escape through one of the three small dark wooden doors not far ahead of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that he had indeed understood but did not choose to trouble himself about it. If he turned round, however, he was caught, for then he would have admitted that he had understood perfectly well, that he really was the person addressed and that he also intended to obey. Had the priest called again, K. would certainly have gone away, but since everything remained silent, however long K. waited, he did turn his head a little after all, for he wished to see what the priest was doing now. He stood quietly in the pulpit as before, but it was plain to see that he had noticed K.’s turning his head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not now turned round completely. He did so and the priest beckoned him nearer with a finger. Since everything could now be done openly, he ran—he did so also out of curiosity and to shorten the business—with long, flying strides towards the pulpit. He halted by the first pews, but the distance still seemed too great to the priest, who stretched out his hand and pointed with his forefinger directed sharply downwards to a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed in this too, at this spot he already had to bend his head far back to keep the priest in view. “You are Josef K.,” said the priest, lifting one hand from the parapet in an indeterminate gesture. “Yes,” said K., he thought of how openly he had always given his name in former times, for some time now it had been a burden to him, and now people whom he was meeting for the first time knew his name; how pleasant it was to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. “You stand accused,” said the priest very softly. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed of it.” “Then you are the man I am looking for,” said the priest. “I am the prison chaplain.” “Oh, I see,” said K. “I had you summoned here,” said the priest, “to speak with you.” “I did not know,” said K. “I came here to show an Italian the cathedral.” “Leave aside what is incidental,” said the priest. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?” “No,” answered K., “it is an album of the sights of the town.” “Put it down,” said the priest. K. flung it away so violently that it fell open and slid some distance across the floor with its pages crumpled. “Do you know that your case is going badly?” asked the priest. “It seems so to me too,” said K. “I have made every effort, but so far without success. Admittedly, I have not yet finished the petition.” “How do you imagine it will end?” asked the priest. “Formerly I thought it must end well,” said K., “now I sometimes doubt it myself. I do not know how it will end. Do you?” “No,” said the priest, “but I fear it will end badly. You are held to be guilty. Your case may never get beyond a lower court. For the present at least, your guilt is held to be proved.” “But I am not guilty,” said K. “It is a mistake. How can a human being be guilty at all. We are all human beings here, one like another.” “That is true,” said the priest, “but that is how the guilty are accustomed to speak.” “Are you prejudiced against me too?” asked K. “I am not prejudiced against you,” said the priest. “I thank you,” said K. “But all the others who are concerned in the proceedings are prejudiced against me. They instil it even into those who are not concerned. My position is growing more and more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the priest. “The judgment does not come all at once, the proceedings gradually pass into judgment.” “So that is how it is,” said K., lowering his head. “What do you intend to do next in your case?” asked the priest. “I intend to seek further help,” said K., raising his head to see what the priest thought of this. “There are still certain possibilities I have not made use of.” “You seek too much help from others,” said the priest disapprovingly, “and particularly from women. Do you not see that it is not true help.” “Sometimes, and indeed often, I could agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could induce some women I know to work together on my behalf, I should be bound to prevail. Particularly with this court, which consists almost entirely of woman-hunters. Show the examining magistrate a woman in the distance and he will trample over the court table and the accused merely to get there in time.” The priest bent his head towards the parapet, only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to press him down. What storm might be raging outside? This was no longer a gloomy day, it was already deepest night. None of the stained glass in the great windows could break the dark wall with even a gleam. And just now the verger began extinguishing the candles on the high altar one after another. “Are you angry with me?” K. asked the priest. “Perhaps you do not know what sort of court you serve.” He received no answer. “These are only my own experiences,” said K. Above him all remained silent. “I did not mean to offend you,” said K. Then the priest shouted down to K.: “Can you not see two paces ahead?” It was shouted in anger, but at the same time like someone who sees another falling and, being startled himself, cries out heedlessly and involuntarily.
